title: 8 · StringTokenizer & Math (Deep Dive)
learn:
The story: slicing bread

A sentence is a loaf. A StringTokenizer slices it into pieces called tokens. By default it cuts on whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines). Import java.util.StringTokenizer.

The three methods

hasMoreTokens(): true while pieces remain. nextToken(): returns the next piece and moves on. countTokens(): how many pieces are left (not yet consumed), so it drops as you read. Calling nextToken() with none left throws NoSuchElementException, hence the hasMoreTokens() guard.

Custom delimiters

Pass the cutting characters as a second argument: new StringTokenizer("a,b;c", ",;"). Each character in that string is a delimiter. A third argument true would return the delimiters themselves as tokens.

When to use it

CSV-style lines read from a file, simple command parsing, counting words. It is a legacy class (String.split() is modern) but your syllabus tests it.

The Math class: a free calculator

In java.lang so no import, every method static: call Math.sqrt(16). Key members: pow(b,e) (returns double: Math.pow(2,3) = 8.0), sqrt(n), abs(n), max(a,b), min(a,b), round(n) (nearest whole: round(4.5) = 5, round(-4.5) = -4), ceil(n) (up), floor(n) (down), random() and constants Math.PI, Math.E.

Random numbers made easy

Math.random() gives 0.0 up to but not including 1.0. To get a whole number from low to high: (int)(Math.random() * (high - low + 1)) + low. Dice: (int)(Math.random()*6)+1. Walk through it: random()*6 gives 0.0-5.99, the cast chops to 0-5, +1 makes 1-6.

Return types matter

pow and sqrt return double, so int x = Math.pow(2,3); will not compile: cast it. round(double) returns long, round(float) returns int.
